newsitem.title: UK: Gencor puts premium on overseas expansion -- Maude.
newsitem.headline: Gencor puts premium on overseas expansion -- Maude.

text.p: Mining giant Gencor is putting a high premium on exploration outside of its South African base, executive director Gary Maude told the Global Emerging Markets 96 conference on Thursday.
This year 80 percent of Gencor's exploration budget was focused outside of South Africa with special interest in Latin America, Africa and Indonesia.
In 1987 that figure was just five percent, he said.
In two to three years Gencor hoped to reach more balance in commodities and geographical diversity, Maude said.
Most of Gencor's operations are still based in South Africa with the emphasis on gold mining due to its 100-year history there.
"The result was we had a full pipeline of projects and from 1960 to 1985 Gencor brough a new mine on stream every two years," he said.
"But pipelines take time to build. We are trying to go international but filling the pipeline will take 10, 12, 15 years," he said.
In the meantime, he said, Gencor was looking for junior companies, such as Eldorado of Canada, to work jointly on smaller projects.
"We are looking for elephants but when you find those you also get a lot of mice," he said.
Gencor is eyeing mineral deposits in the Andes and in Indonesia there are very prospective gold and copper desposits.
The company is also interested in the Caribbean region for nickel deposits, he added.
"The story of the internationalisation of Gencor is just starting. South Africa came late but I predict they will still make their mark," he said.
By the year 2000, Gencor's goal was to be ranked first in ferro alloys and coal exports, second in platinum and mineral sands, third in coal production and fourth in gold.
Referring to Russian platinum exports, he said "I think most of it is from stocks."
Maude said the decline in gold output facing South African producers originated from structural issues which had no easy solutions such as educating the adult workforce.
"I can see a lot of benefit in adult education and training but the implied question is can we make deep level gold mining significantly more efficient. What is against us is the cost," he said.
